belongs_to: Fig. 5.1 - "Take a piece of square paper and fold it in different ways ... draw lines on the creases"
description: A square sheet drawn with a solid black outline and 7 dashed crease lines, no letters, no angle values. (1) Two vertical dashed lines, full height, at about 20% and 60% of the width from the left edge. (2) One horizontal dashed line across the full width at about the middle of the height (about 51%). (3) One almost-horizontal dashed line across the full width that starts on the left edge just below the middle line (about 54% of the height) and ends on the right edge lower (about 60% of the height), so it slopes slightly downward to the right. (4) Two corner-to-corner dashed diagonals (top-left to bottom-right, and bottom-left to top-right), crossing at the centre where a tiny "x" mark is printed. (5) One more dashed oblique line that starts on the left edge at about 60% of the height and goes up to the right to meet the top edge at about 77% of the width from the left. The lines cross each other in several places inside the sheet; none of them is labelled.
unclear: Exact percentages are read by eye from the picture; the count of 7 dashed lines was checked edge by edge (left edge 5 ends, right edge 4, top edge 5, bottom edge 4).

belongs_to: Fig. 5.2 - "line l intersects line m, four angles are formed"; "In Fig. 5.2, if angle a is 120 degrees, can you figure out b, c, d?"; linear pairs
description: Two straight lines crossing at one point, both drawn with arrowheads at both ends. Line l is horizontal (label l near its right end, above the line). Line m rises from the lower left (arrowhead) to the upper right (arrowhead), crossing l at the middle (label m above the upper-right part). Four angles are marked with small arcs and a letter each: angle a in the upper-left region (between the left half of l and the upper half of m), RED arc, obtuse; angle b in the upper-right region (between the upper half of m and the right half of l), BLACK arc, acute; angle c in the lower-right region, RED arc, obtuse (it is the vertically opposite angle of a); angle d in the lower-left region, BLACK arc, acute (opposite to b). No degree values are printed on the figure (the text uses a = 120 degrees, b = 60 degrees). Caption "Fig. 5.2".

belongs_to: Fig. 5.3 - "List all the linear pairs and vertically opposite angles you observe in Fig. 5.3"
description: Two straight lines crossing at one point, both with arrowheads at both ends and both steep. Line l runs from the top-left (arrowhead) to the bottom-right (arrowhead), label l near its lower-right end; line m runs from the bottom-left (arrowhead) to the top-right (arrowhead), label m near its lower-left end. Four angles around the crossing: b at the top (BLACK arc, narrow angle, label b above the arc); a on the left (RED arc, wide angle, label a to the left of the arc); c on the right (RED arc, wide angle, label c to the right); d at the bottom (BLACK arc, narrow angle, label d below the arc). So the two RED arcs mark the wide pair a and c, the two BLACK arcs mark the narrow pair b and d. No degree values printed. Caption "Fig. 5.3".

belongs_to: Table printed beside Fig. 5.3 for the answer to "List all the linear pairs and vertically opposite angles"
description: A 2-row by 2-column table with a red border and red grid lines, no colour fills. Row 1: left cell "Linear Pairs", right cell "angle a and angle b, ..." (printed as "∠a and ∠b, …"). Row 2: left cell "Pairs of Vertically Opposite Angles" (on two lines), right cell "angle b and angle d, ..." (printed as "∠b and ∠d, …"). The right cells hold the first example of each list, to be continued by the student.

belongs_to: Fig. 5.4 - "In Fig. 5.4, we can say that lines l and m are perpendicular to each other"
description: Two straight lines crossing at right angles, both with arrowheads at both ends. Line m is nearly horizontal, rising to the right (about 18 degrees), label m above its upper-right end; line l is steep, running from the upper-left (arrowhead) to the lower-right (arrowhead), label l near its lower end. A small square right-angle mark sits in the upper-right region at the crossing, between the upper part of l and the right part of m. No degree value printed. Caption "Fig. 5.4".

belongs_to: Fig. 5.5 - "Observe Fig. 5.5 and describe the way the line segments meet or cross each other ... ST and UV, OP and QR likely to meet if extended?"
description: Eleven labelled points drawn as filled blue-violet dots joined into 8 line segments (all segments have dots as endpoints, no arrowheads). (1) Segment ST and (2) segment UV, one above the other, both rising to the right: S (left) to T (upper right), U (lower left, just below S and a little right) to V (right). They look nearly parallel but UV is slightly steeper (about 23 degrees against about 20 degrees for ST), so they slowly come together to the right. T and V are the right ends; V sits just below-right of T. (3) Segment OP: O (upper left) to P (lower right), falling to the right at about 33 degrees. (4) Segment QR: Q (left of O, a little lower) to R (far lower right), falling at the same slope; QR is longer than OP (about twice as long) and lies below-left of OP. OP and QR look parallel. (5) Segment AB: A (left) to B (upper right) rising at about 44 degrees; (6) segment CD: C (upper left) to D (lower right, slightly falling). AB and CD cross each other at a point labelled X (label X sits just below-left of the crossing). X is at about the middle of CD, and about 60% of the way from A to B (nearer B). (7) Segment IJ: I (upper left) to J (lower right, falling at 45 degrees); (8) segment LM: L (upper right) to M (lower left, rising about 35 degrees). IJ and LM cross at a point labelled Y (label Y just above the crossing); Y is at about the middle of IJ and of LM (roughly 54% of the way along each). Separate from those: segments FG and FH meet at the common endpoint F; F is upper left, H is to the right of F and slightly higher, G is below F and slightly left. A small arc at F between FH and FG carries the label 115.3 degrees (printed "115.3°") written below-right of the arc. Letters sit next to their dots: S left of its dot, T above, V right, U below-left; Q above-left, O above, P right, R right; B upper right, C upper left, D lower right, A left; I above-left, L right, J lower right, M below; F above-left, H above-right, G below-left. Caption "Fig. 5.5". The points are scattered on the page (no grid).
unclear: Angles of the segments in degrees and the fractions along AB/CD/IJ/LM are measured from the picture and are approximate.
It is not certain that X and Y are exact midpoints.

belongs_to: "What is common to the lines in the pictures above? They do not seem likely to intersect each other. Such lines are called parallel lines."
description: Three small pictures side by side, each in a black frame, showing real-life parallel lines. (1) A piano keyboard seen from above, tilted a little (its front edge slopes down to the right): white keys separated by thin lines, 10 black keys in groups of 2, 3, 2, 3 (from left to right). (2) A red park bench on a green background, front view: a backrest of 12 vertical slats including the two end posts (11 narrow gaps between them), a top rail, a seat, and legs. (3) A railway track seen from above on a white frame: two dark horizontal rails (top and bottom of a band), 6 brown wooden sleepers standing vertically between them, with grey gravel stones between the sleepers (7 stretches of gravel).
unclear: Number of white piano keys not counted (the picture is cropped and low resolution).

belongs_to: "Name some parallel lines you can spot in your classroom. ... Parallel lines are often used in artwork and shading."
description: Two small framed pictures side by side. unclear: Decorative art; the exact count of strips/stripes was not counted. Listed because the text points at it as an example of parallel lines in artwork.

belongs_to: Fig. 5.6 - "Which pairs of lines appear to be parallel in Fig. 5.6 below?"

Coordinates below are (column, row) counting from 0 at the top-left dot, columns 0 to 15 left to right, rows 0 to 7 top to bottom. Nine black line segments, each with dots as end points and a lowercase italic letter beside it: a = vertical, from (1,0) down to (1,3), 3 units, letter a to its left; c = horizontal, from (1,3) to (9,3), 8 units (it starts at the foot of a, so a and c form an L), letter c above it between columns 2 and 3; d = diagonal going down to the right, from (3,1) to (6,4), 3 units, letter d to its upper right; e = diagonal going up to the right, from (6,4) to (9,1), 3 units, letter e to its upper left (d and e together make a V with the point at (6,4)); b = diagonal going up to the right, from (1,6) to (4,3), 3 units, letter b to its upper left (its top end lies on c); g = horizontal, from (5,4) to (12,4), 7 units, letter g above it near column 10; f = long diagonal going down to the right, from (9,3) to (13,7), 4 units (it starts at the right end of c and crosses g at (10,4)), letter f on its right near row 5; h = vertical, from (8,4) down to (8,7), 3 units, letter h to its right (starts on g); i = vertical, from (5,4) down to (5,7), 3 units, letter i to its right (starts at the left end of g). Reading the coordinates: a, h, i are vertical; c and g horizontal; b and e rise at 45 degrees; d and f fall at 45 degrees. Caption "Fig. 5.6".

belongs_to: Fig. 5.7 - Activity 2: "Fold the sheet horizontally in half. A new line is formed (see Fig. 5.7)"; "Make one more horizontal fold ... How many parallel lines do you see now?"
description: A sequence of 8 small panels in 4 rows and 2 columns, each a thin-outlined square (or folded rectangle) with dashed creases and blue curved arrows. Row 1: left = square sheet with 1 horizontal dashed line across the middle and a blue arrow curving downward (fold the top half down); right = the unfolded square with 1 horizontal dashed crease. Row 2: left = the folded sheet, a rectangle of half the height with a small flap line on the right edge, 1 horizontal dashed line across its middle and a blue arrow pointing down (second fold); right = the unfolded square with 3 horizontal dashed creases (equally spaced, at 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 of the height). Row 3: left = a narrow strip (a quarter of the height) with its flap on the right edge, 1 dashed line along the middle and a blue arrow pointing down (third fold); right = the unfolded square with 7 horizontal dashed creases (equally spaced, 8 strips). Row 4: left = square with the 7 horizontal dashed creases and a vertical thin line through the middle, with a blue arrow curving to the right across it (the vertical fold); right = the same square with the 7 horizontal dashed creases and 1 vertical crease line through the middle (drawn dashed). So the number of parallel horizontal creases goes 1, 3, 7 after one, two, three folds. Caption "Fig. 5.7".

belongs_to: Fig. 5.8 - second paper-folding activity: "Fold the top right and bottom left corners onto the creased line to create triangles ... Are a, b and c parallel to p, q and r respectively? Why or why not?"
description: A sequence of 6 small panels in 3 rows and 2 columns, each a thin-outlined square sheet; blue curved arrows show the folds. Row 1: left = square with 1 vertical dashed crease in the middle and a blue arrow curving to the right across it; right = the square with that 1 vertical dashed crease. Row 2: left = square with 3 vertical dashed creases (at 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 of the width) and two blue arrows pointing towards the centre, one from the left (pointing right) and one from the right (pointing left), the edges folded in to the centre line; right = the square with the 3 vertical dashed creases. Row 3 left: the same 3 creases; the top-right corner is folded down to the third crease and shows a grey right-angled triangle whose vertical edge (on the third crease line) is labelled a, whose horizontal edge (below the folded part, along the right edge) is labelled b, and whose sloping fold edge at the top right is labelled c; the bottom-left corner is folded up and shows a grey right-angled triangle whose horizontal top edge is labelled q, whose vertical right edge (on the first crease line) is labelled p, and whose sloping fold edge at the lower left is labelled r. In this panel a is vertical like p, b is horizontal like q, c slopes down to the right like r. Row 3 right: the same sheet with the two corners folded so that the grey triangles are narrow slivers pointing inward (top-right sliver with a at its left, b at its lower right, c at its upper right; bottom-left sliver with q above, r on its left and p on its right). Caption "Fig. 5.8".
unclear: The exact edge each of a, b, c, p, q, r points to in the right-hand panel of row 3 is hard to read (small labels on thin triangles); the left-hand panel is clear.

belongs_to: Fig. 5.9 - "we use an arrow mark (>) to show that a set of lines is parallel ... second set shown with two arrow marks ... Perpendicular lines are marked with a square angle"

(1) Top left: two horizontal parallel line segments one above the other, each carrying ONE arrowhead mark (">") near its right end, pointing right. belongs_to: Q4 - "Using your sense of how parallel lines look, try to draw lines parallel to the line segments on this dot paper" (Fig. 5.12)

belongs_to: Q5 - "In Fig. 5.13, which line is parallel to line a - line b or line c? How do you decide this?"
description: Five blue-violet dots joined by four black segments, no grid. Call the dots (x, y) in the picture frame: top T, left L, bottom B, middle-right M, far-right R. Segments: line a = L to B, from the left dot down-right to the bottom dot (falling at about 31 degrees), letter a below it; line b = T to R, from the top dot to the far-right dot, the longest, falling at about 28 degrees, letter b above its right part; line c = T to M, from the same top dot to the middle-right dot (which lies slightly below line b), falling at about 32 degrees, letter c below it near the middle; and one more segment from T straight down to B, steep (falling at about 61 degrees), with no letter. Lines b and c start at the same top dot and make a very narrow angle with each other; a looks parallel to c (32 versus 31 degrees) rather than to b (28 degrees). Caption "Fig. 5.13".
unclear: The letters b and c are assigned to the two long segments by label position: b above the right part of the longer line, c below the middle of the shorter line. The steep segment T-B has no letter.
Angles are measured from the picture and are approximate.

belongs_to: Fig. 5.14 - "line t intersects lines l and m. t is called a transversal. Notice that 8 angles are formed"; vertically opposite angles; corresponding angles 1 and 5, 2 and 6, 3 and 7, 4 and 8
description: Two lines l and m cut by a transversal t, all with arrowheads at both ends. l is nearly horizontal, sloping slightly down to the right (label l above its right end); m is nearly horizontal, sloping slightly UP to the right (label m above its right end), so l and m are not parallel (they come closer to the right); t is steep, leaning to the right going up (label t at its lower end). Eight angles numbered with plain digits, no arcs and no degree values. At the crossing of t with l: 1 upper-left, 2 upper-right, 3 lower-right, 4 lower-left. At the crossing of t with m: 5 upper-left, 6 upper-right, 7 lower-right, 8 lower-left. Caption "Fig. 5.14".
